title: JavaScript Promises 101
description: A short, hands-on course that takes you from callback confusion to confident async/await.
goal: Be able to read, write, and debug asynchronous JavaScript using Promises and async/await.

units.title: Why Asynchronous JavaScript?
units.goal: Explain why JavaScript needs asynchronous code and what the event loop does at a high level.

teacherBrain.persona: A patient senior engineer who teaches with small concrete examples.
objectives: Make the learner comfortable with the idea of non-blocking code.
Connect blocking vs non-blocking to real user-facing latency.
guidelines: Ask a quick check-for-understanding question after each new idea.
Ground explanations in the provided knowledge chunks.
constraints: Do not introduce async/await yet — that is a later unit.
Do not dump large code blocks; keep examples under 8 lines.
Never invent APIs that are not standard JavaScript.
teacherBrain.systemPromptSeed: You are teaching the very first unit. Assume the learner knows basic synchronous JS only.

knowledgeBaseChunks.title: Blocking vs non-blocking
knowledgeBaseChunks.content: JavaScript runs on a single thread. A blocking operation (like a long synchronous loop) freezes everything else, including the UI. Non-blocking operations hand work off and let the engine keep responding to other events.

knowledgeBaseChunks.title: The event loop in one paragraph
knowledgeBaseChunks.content: The event loop continuously checks: is the call stack empty? If so, it takes the next queued callback (from timers, network, etc.) and runs it. This is how single-threaded JS can wait for many things at once without blocking.

knowledgeBaseChunks.title: Why callbacks were the first answer
knowledgeBaseChunks.content: Before Promises, asynchronous results were delivered via callback functions passed into APIs like setTimeout or XMLHttpRequest. Nesting many callbacks led to deeply indented 'callback hell'.

questions.prompt: In your own words, what happens to the UI when a long synchronous loop runs on the main thread?
questions.answer: The UI freezes because the single thread is busy with the loop and cannot process other events until it finishes.

hints.text: Think about how many threads run your JS by default.
If the one thread is busy, what can't it do?

questions.prompt: Which best describes the event loop's job?
options: It adds more threads when JS is busy.
It runs queued callbacks when the call stack is empty.
It compiles JavaScript to machine code.
It blocks the page until network requests finish.
questions.answer: It runs queued callbacks when the call stack is empty.

hints.text: It is about scheduling, not threads or compilation.

commonMistakes.mistake: Believing JavaScript is multi-threaded because async code 'runs in parallel'.
commonMistakes.correction: JS executes on one main thread; concurrency comes from the event loop scheduling callbacks, not from parallel threads.

units.title: Promises, Step by Step
units.goal: Create and consume a Promise, and chain .then()/.catch() correctly.

teacherBrain.persona: A patient senior engineer who teaches with small concrete examples.
objectives: Teach the three Promise states and how they transition.
Get the learner chaining .then() and handling errors with .catch().
guidelines: Show a tiny runnable example for each concept.
Always pair a .then() example with its .catch() counterpart.
Reference the knowledge chunks rather than improvising semantics.
constraints: Keep async/await out of this unit unless the learner explicitly asks.
Do not skip error handling — it is part of the goal.

knowledgeBaseChunks.title: The three states of a Promise
knowledgeBaseChunks.content: A Promise is always in one of three states: pending (not settled yet), fulfilled (resolved with a value), or rejected (failed with a reason). Once settled it never changes state again.

knowledgeBaseChunks.title: then, catch, finally
knowledgeBaseChunks.content: .then(onFulfilled) runs when the promise resolves. .catch(onRejected) runs when it rejects. .finally() runs either way. Each .then() returns a new promise, which is what makes chaining possible.

knowledgeBaseChunks.title: Creating a promise
knowledgeBaseChunks.content: new Promise((resolve, reject) => { ... }) gives you a settle function pair. Call resolve(value) on success or reject(error) on failure. Most of the time you consume promises returned by APIs rather than constructing your own.

questions.prompt: What are the three states a Promise can be in?

hints.text: One before it settles, two after.

questions.prompt: Why does .then() let you chain another .then() after it?
questions.answer: Because .then() itself returns a new promise, so you can attach another handler to that returned promise.

hints.text: Chaining works because each link is itself a promise.

commonMistakes.mistake: Forgetting to return a value or promise inside a .then(), which breaks the chain.
commonMistakes.correction: Always return from a .then() callback if the next .then() depends on its result.

commonMistakes.mistake: Omitting .catch(), so rejected promises fail silently.
commonMistakes.correction: Attach a .catch() (or a trailing error handler) to every chain so rejections are handled.
